cards.back: Moving as few bytes as possible, keeping many devices in step, and never losing or corrupting anything.

cards.front: Change rate for 100M daily users making 10 changes each
cards.back: About 1B a day, roughly 12k a second, peaking around 3× in working hours.

cards.front: Block references for 1 EB in 4 MB blocks
cards.back: 250 billion, each a 32-byte hash plus bookkeeping: tens of TB of metadata that must be sharded.
Ask which block hashes are missing, upload only those via presigned URLs, then commit the list of hashes with the parent revision.

cards.front: What a block's SHA-256 hash is used for
cards.back: Its name, its dedupe key and its integrity check.

cards.front: Why a 50 GB upload is resumable
cards.back: It is 12,500 independent 4 MB block uploads, each retried on its own.
Inserting a byte near the start shifts every fixed block boundary; content-defined chunking places boundaries by a rolling hash, so only the touched block changes.
An instant upload tells the uploader someone already has that file. Services often limit dedupe to an account or team.
Each namespace has an append-only journal with sequence numbers; a device remembers the last one applied and fetches entries after it.
Nothing but 'there are changes'. A lost notification only delays sync; the journal guarantees nothing is missed.

cards.front: How conflicts are detected and resolved
cards.back: Commits are compare-and-set on parent_rev. On conflict the losing client saves a conflicted copy next to the winner, so no edit is silently lost.

cards.front: Why deleting a file doesn't delete its blocks
cards.back: Blocks may be shared. Keep reference counts and delete unreferenced blocks after the version-history window, often 30+ days.

quiz.q: A user inserts one sentence near the start of a 2 GB file and the client re-uploads almost the whole file. Why?
choices: The server lost the old blocks
Fixed-size blocks shifted, changing every hash after the insert
quiz.why: Content-defined chunking keeps boundaries with the content so only one block changes.

quiz.q: Two laptops edit the same spreadsheet offline and both sync. What should the system do?
choices: Merge the files byte by byte
Accept the first commit and save the second as a conflicted copy
quiz.why: Compare-and-set detects it and both versions are kept so no work is lost.

quiz.q: A device was offline for two weeks. How does it catch up?
choices: Calls /changes with its stored cursor and downloads missing blocks
Waits for push notifications to replay
quiz.why: The cursor works however long it was away; a compacted journal falls back to a full listing.

quiz.q: A buggy client release starts deleting files on every device of an account. What limits the damage?
choices: Version history plus server-side rate limits on bulk deletes
quiz.why: Versions let files be restored and delete limits stop the spread.

quiz.q: A user copies a 1 GB installer that thousands of others already uploaded. What does the client send?
choices: Only the block hashes; no blocks are missing so nothing is uploaded
quiz.why: Content-addressed blocks dedupe identical content (subject to dedupe scope).

quiz.q: A downloaded file's block doesn't match its stored SHA-256. What is the right response?
choices: Ignore it if the size matches
Alert immediately and repair from a replica
quiz.why: Hash mismatches mean corruption; verify at every hop and repair from replicas.

quiz.q: Why do file bytes go to the block store through presigned URLs instead of the API?
choices: To keep large transfers off API servers so metadata and bytes scale separately
Because the API can't handle HTTPS
quiz.why: Metadata calls, block transfers and notifications are separate flows.
